passage:
On Tuesday, Anirban said to his mother, "Mummy, I'll finish my drawing in ten minutes, well before we eat." He got out all his colours and began a big picture of a train station. At the first hour he was still adding tiny windows. When Mummy Preeti called him for dinner, he wailed that it was not done yet, and his eyes filled with tears as he left the page half-coloured.
On Wednesday, Sonali Ma'am reminded the class that the science project on plants was due on Friday. "That will take me ten minutes," Anirban told his friend. He did not begin on Wednesday, and he did not begin on Thursday afternoon. On Thursday night, at eight o'clock, he opened the chart paper and found he had no glue, no pictures and no idea where to begin. He remembered how easy the plan had looked in his head, while the paper in front of him looked huge. Mummy Preeti found him at the table at nine, sighing, with the pen cap in his mouth. Nobody had told him to think of Tuesday's drawing, and he had not remembered it himself.

qa.q: What did Anirban tell his mother he would finish before dinner?
qa.a: He said he would finish his drawing in ten minutes.

qa.q: How do Tuesday's drawing and Thursday night's project show the same mistake?
qa.a: Both times Anirban imagined a task taking ten minutes and pictured the easy path. On Tuesday the drawing stretched to an hour and ended in tears; on Thursday he began the plant project late and forgot how long the drawing had really taken.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when Mummy Preeti called him to dinner with the drawing unfinished?
qa.a: He felt upset and frustrated, because he had expected to be done and now had to stop halfway.

qa.q: What could Anirban do next time he plans a task?
qa.a: He could remember how long the drawing really took, add extra time, and begin the project earlier in small parts.

grounding: The same boy imagines a task will take ten minutes (3650) and it stretches into an hour with tears (7655), then repeats the misjudgement on a school project.
